transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Recording: auto
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rohit Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Lina Ortega (Eldritch Head of ML), Samir Qureshi (Cloud Eng), Avery Cole (Security)

Summary: quick intro, then deep into networking constraints and pilot success metrics. Lots of back-and-forth on whether VPC peering or PrivateLink is feasible given their M&A firewall inspection footprint.

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick intros, i'm maya, i'm the account lead on this one for Redwood inference.
[00:00:10] Lina: hi, lina here, head of ml at Eldritch Biosciences, thanks for doing this.
[00:00:14] Samir: samir, cloud engineer, i'll be owning the VPC peering bits.
[00:00:18] Avery: avery, security — i'll be the compliance point.
[00:00:22] Rohit: and i'm rohit, systems engineer, i'll run the benchmark and help with network setup.

[00:01:05] Maya: the goal today is to scope a pilot — a private networking + residency POC — so we understand success criteria, what to benchmark, and the timeline. We'll propose 3 benchmark configs: hosted private, dedicated reserved, and private (customer VPC) with Peering/PrivateLink variants.
[00:01:26] Lina: right, the non-negotiable for us is that model inference and any request/response payloads must not leave the EU. We also have deep packet inspection on the egress so static egress IPs or a closed peering tunnel are kinda mandatory.
[00:01:45] Samir: to add, we have an inspection appliance that only allows traffic to a list of IPs. we can do VPC peering but our firewalls do additional inspection on egress and NAT, so we need consistent IPs to pass the rules.
[00:02:10] Rohit: got it. two common options: VPC peering (cross-account peering) or AWS PrivateLink. peering gives you full L3 connectivity but you have to manage routes and there can be issues with overlapping CIDRs. PrivateLink is cleaner from an egress/IP perspective because you can front with NLBs and maintain managed endpoints. however PrivateLink can add per-GB costs and requires some infra setup.
[00:02:35] Avery: what's the difference for audit logs and KMS usage? if data never leaves EU but the control plane is outside, is that acceptable?
[00:02:45] Maya: our Private deployment can be placed in customer-managed VPC in eu-west-1; the control plane can be in our zone but we support a private control plane option for enterprise so audit logs and model artifacts can remain customer-side. we support customer-managed KMS, which we can integrate for key wrapping. sometimes the wording in the docs gets messy so sorry if i say cms instead of kms earlier, my bad.
[00:03:10] Lina: okay, we need KMS integration and audit logs retained for 1 year. also are you able to support a locked region mode? we can't have automatic fallback to other regions.
[00:03:25] Rohit: yes we can lock routes — routing policy can force eu-only execution. fallback is configurable; for the pilot we'd set strict region enforcement and no cross-region fallback.
[00:03:40] Samir: ping: is there a way to put the Redwood runtime inside our private subnet and still have telemetry out? we want metrics but all telemetry must cross an inspection gateway.
[00:03:50] Rohit: telemetry can be forwarded over your egress to an internal metrics collector — we can also buffer and ship logs via customer-managed S3 endpoints. in Private deployments we give control over where metrics go.
[00:04:10] Lina: success criteria from our side: latency P95 < 200ms for short prompts (<= 128 tokens), sustained throughput to handle spiky workloads (target 2000 tokens/sec spiky bursts), error rate < 1% over 24h, and cost per 1M tokens to be under our threshold — if cost is too high we'll need to evaluate quantization or batching changes.
[00:04:45] Maya: that aligns with typical pilot metrics. we'll design benchmarks to measure cold-start, warm steady-state, and sustained heavy load. our SE will propose three configs: small-batch low-latency (single caller optimized), throughput-batched, and quantized model baseline.
[00:05:10] Rohit: i'll include spike tests, a steady-scan over 2 hours, and a longer 24h run to capture error modes. can you share typical request size distributions? average tokens per request, 99th percentile?
[00:05:25] Samir: we have histograms, i'll export them — avg payload is about 80 tokens, p95 is 380 when people send long clinical notes, but those are rare. most traffic is short.
[00:05:42] Lina: also note we have some latency-sensitive endpoints that rely on sub-200ms turnaround. those are low QPS but very sensitive.
[00:05:50] Rohit: understood. we'll include targeted microbenchmarks for those endpoints.

[00:06:30] Maya: network specifics: for peering we'll need your VPC CIDRs and allowed peering routes. for PrivateLink we'll provide an NLB in the provider account and you'll attach endpoints — that gives you a fixed set of ENIs and predictable egress. which approach do you prefer?
[00:06:50] Samir: peering is okay if we can avoid CIDR overlap and if egress IPs are stable. our ops are more familiar with peering. but PrivateLink may be easier for us to audit since it uses endpoint ENIs. the cost side matters too.
[00:07:10] Maya: cost-wise PrivateLink has additional data processing charges but reduces NAT-gateway egress unpredictability. we'll include estimated networking cost in the pilot pricing.
[00:07:25] Avery: one concern: our DLP stack requires TLS inspection on egress. if traffic is fully encrypted end-to-end to your runtime, our inspection can't peer inside. do you allow mirrored telemetry so we can match requests to responses without decrypting?
[00:07:40] Rohit: for Private deployments you control the keys and can host the runtime; the traffic inside your VPC can be unencrypted between your internal proxy and runtime if your policy allows, but we recommend mTLS. we can also provide hashed request identifiers in logs so you can correlate without plaintext. small transcription note: earlier i said k-v cache as 'k v cash' — apologies for the verbal slip.
[00:08:10] Lina: we also have a third-party vendor that requires a static egress IP to allow API calls back to their service. can you support assigning a fixed egress IP from Redwood side?
[00:08:22] Maya: on hosted mode, we can't guarantee single static IP per customer globally; with Dedicated or Private deployment we can provide NAT through an audited egress gateway with static IPs in the region. for PrivateLink, the egress tends to be on your side so it's simpler.
[00:08:40] Samir: good — Dedicated could work if costs fit. what's a typical timeline for standing up a Private pilot in eu-west-1?
[00:08:50] Maya: typically 2-4 weeks to provision Dedicated capacity plus network setup, longer if you want private control plane (4-6 weeks). for a tight POC we aim for a 4-week pilot.
[00:09:04] Rohit: bench timeline: week 1 — infra + connectivity (peering/PrivateLink), week 2 — smoke tests and small bench, week 3 — full perf bench (latency, p95, throughput), week 4 — 24h soak and results.
[00:09:20] Lina: OK. on the security side, Avery, are there any blockers?
[00:09:26] Avery: SOC2 report availability is okay; we need to validate SIEM ingestion and key management. also we need to confirm the private control plane option if we require air-gap in later stage. for the POC we'll accept a partial control plane so long as no inference data leaves EU.
[00:09:42] Maya: noted. we'll provide SOC2 docs and the private control plane design doc.

[00:10:30] Samir: quick technical Q: how does prefix caching/KV cache behave over peering vs PrivateLink? if we have a long context window, we want to cache KV state inside our VPC to reduce cross-account calls.
[00:10:45] Rohit: the KV cache is part of the runtime — in Private deployments the cache lives inside the customer's runtime by default. over peering, you can configure affinity so hot KV loads stay local for a given shard. there is some nuance with sharding and sticky routing — we'll include recommendations.
[00:11:10] Lina: will you support quantized model variants in the pilot? some of our cost targets require 4-bit quantization acceptable quality tradeoff.
[00:11:18] Rohit: yes, we can run quantized variants and measure quality regressions against your eval set. Redwood Optimize will provide quantization recommendations and we can log sample diffs.
[00:11:30] Maya: let's capture success criteria explicitly: 1) P95 latency < 200ms for <=128 token prompts, 2) sustained throughput target of 2000 tokens/sec for burst windows, 3) error rate <1% over 24h, 4) no data exfiltration outside eu-west-1, 5) integration with customer KMS for key wrapping. sound right?
[00:11:55] Lina: yes, and add cost target: cost per 1M tokens < our limit — i'll share the number offline.
[00:12:02] Maya: noted.

[00:12:40] Samir: about endpoints and DNS: for PrivateLink we would point an internal DNS name to the endpoint. is there a recommended TTL? our security likes short TTLs but we want stability during bench runs.
[00:12:53] Rohit: recommend 60 seconds TTL for test, 300s for steady-state. PrivateLink ENIs are stable so longer TTL is fine once tested.
[00:13:10] Avery: what about transport security and mTLS rotation? we need cert rotation policies to meet our internal audits.
[00:13:18] Rohit: we support mTLS with automated rotation windows; certs can be managed by your KMS or by Redwood-managed certs if you prefer. we'll document rotation timelines.

[00:14:05] Maya: i want to call out the bench configs we'll run: A) Single-node low-latency: small batch sizes, minimal batching, measure cold/warm P95; B) Throughput-batched: larger batch sizes to maximize tokens/sec; C) Quantized model baseline: run quantized variant to measure cost/quality tradeoff. each will have a steady-state and spike component.
[00:14:30] Lina: can we also include a canary path for critical endpoints that uses a pinned model version? we need deterministic behavior during experiments.
[00:14:37] Rohit: yes, model pinning and rollout control are part of the runtime; we'll pin a single model build for the pilot.

[00:15:10] Samir: on network setup, i'll need a prescriptive diagram and a terraform example for peering and for PrivateLink.
[00:15:16] Maya: rohit will share both and a minimal CloudFormation example.
[00:15:22] Rohit: yes. i'll include ips, route tables, security group examples, and a sample NLB config.

[00:16:00] Avery: from a compliance perspective, we'll need to map data flows to our DLP control points. can you provide request/response pseudonymization options or hashed ids?
[00:16:12] Rohit: we support hashed request ids and sample redaction piping to S3 that you can control. we can also support partial tokenization if you want to scrub PHI before transmission. we'll need to scope that as it affects latency.
[00:16:35] Lina: we don't want to add too many proxies in the critical path. maybe for POC we do hashed ids and redaction outside the hotpath.
[00:16:44] Maya: agreed — we'll keep the hotpath minimal and document optional scrub steps for later phases.

[00:17:30] (cross-talk)
[00:17:36] Maya: quick check: pricing sensitivity — do you have a budget range for pilot or a cap?
[00:17:45] Lina: we have a pilot budget but it's modest; we need to compare Dedicated vs Private. cost per token matters.
[00:17:53] Maya: we'll put together a simple cost projection with estimated networking and model costs for each bench config.

[00:18:10] Samir: timelines: if we move quickly and share histograms this week, can we start infra next week?
[00:18:17] Maya: yes — assuming VPC info and SOC2 docs, we can kick infra provisioning next week.

[00:18:40] Rohit: one more technical flag: if you have strict egress inspection, prefer PrivateLink because it avoids NAT bounce that can change source IPs. PrivateLink endpoints present stable ENIs in your subnet which the inspection appliance can see.
[00:19:00] Samir: noted. that helps.

[00:19:30] Maya: ok let's recap and agree on owners.
[00:19:35] Maya: Redwood will: share network diagrams and terraform examples (rohit), send SOC2 and control plane doc (maya), provide benchmark plan and instrumentation (rohit).
[00:19:50] Samir: Eldritch will: send request size histograms and VPC/CIDR info (samir), confirm compliance items and KMS preference (avery), and share the cost cap for pilot (lina).
[00:20:05] Lina: we'll try to get those to you by friday.
[00:20:09] Maya: perfect. we'll schedule the bench kickoff and i'll send calendar invites.

[00:20:40] Rohit: small note: we'll need 1-2 dedicated GPUs for a stable bench — i'll include instance sizing recommendations.
[00:20:50] Maya: thanks. anything else?
[00:20:55] Avery: just one, are backups of model artifacts allowed in our s3? we want to ensure encryption at rest with our KMS.
[00:21:03] Rohit: yes, snapshots and artifacts can be stored in your S3 with your KMS.

[00:21:30] (wrap-up)
[00:21:35] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and next steps.
[00:21:40] Lina: thank you.
[00:21:42] Samir: thanks all.
[00:21:45] Avery: thanks.

End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (KMS noted as CMS in one spot), some speaker overlaps and brief crosstalk. The transcript contains paraphrases for some technical items rather than verbatim code snippets.
